statement: Assume the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). Then some set $V \subseteq [0,1]$ is not measurable for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure).

hypotheses.text: The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) holds.

conclusion: Some set $V \subseteq [0,1]$ is not Lebesgue measurable.

proofs.name: Rational translates
proofs.slogan: Choose one point from each class of reals that differ by a rational, and cover $[0,1]$ by countably many disjoint translates of this set.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $V \subseteq [0,1]$. The choice step uses the axiom of choice, and the argument builds no set without it.

roles.why: Choice picks one point from each of the uncountably many classes.

steps.slogan: Split the reals into classes of numbers that differ by a rational.
steps.detail: Write $x \sim y$ when $x - y$ is a [rational number](c:rational-number). This is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation). Its classes are the cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$, the points of the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Q}$, and each class meets $[0,1]$.

steps.slogan: Choose one point of $[0,1]$ from each class to form the set $V$.
steps.detail: The axiom of choice gives a set $V \subseteq [0,1]$ with exactly one point in each class. Then every real $x$ has exactly one $v \in V$ with $x - v \in \mathbb{Q}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the rational translates of $V$ cover $[0,1]$ and lie in $[-1,2]$.
steps.detail: List the [countable](c:countable-set) set $\mathbb{Q} \cap [-1,1]$ as $q_1, q_2, \dots$ and put $V_j = V + q_j$. A point $x \in [0,1]$ has some $v \in V \subseteq [0,1]$ with $x - v \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [-1,1]$, so $x$ lies in some $V_j$. Each $V_j$ lies in $[-1,2]$.

steps.slogan: Show that two different translates of $V$ are disjoint.
steps.detail: Suppose $v + q_i = v' + q_j$ with $v, v' \in V$. Then $v - v'$ is rational, so $v = v'$ by the choice of $V$, and hence $q_i = q_j$.

steps.slogan: Compare the measure of the union with the measure of $V$.
steps.detail: If $V$ were measurable, every $V_j$ would have the same measure $m$ by translation invariance of [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). Countable additivity gives $1 \le \sum_j m \le 3$. This fails for $m = 0$ (the sum is $0$) and for $m > 0$ (the sum is infinite).

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice selects one representative from each class without a rule.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Translation invariance and countable additivity of the measure give the contradiction.
concepts.c:rational-number: Differences by rationals define the classes of the construction.
concepts.c:equivalence-relation: The relation splits the reals into disjoint classes.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The classes are the points of the quotient group of the reals by the rationals.
concepts.c:countable-set: Only countably many rational translates are used, so additivity applies.

source.note: Vitali's construction of 1905, as in Royden, Real Analysis, in the chapter on Lebesgue measure.

statement: Let a [path integral](c:path-integral) with weight $e^{iS/\hbar}$ have an invariant measure and a [continuous symmetry](c:continuous-symmetry) $\phi \mapsto \phi + \varepsilon\,\delta\phi$ with current $j^\mu$. Then $\langle \partial_\mu j^\mu(x)\,\phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)\rangle = -i\hbar \sum_k \delta(x - x_k)\,\langle \phi(x_1)\cdots\delta\phi(x_k)\cdots\phi(x_n)\rangle$.

hypotheses.text: The action is invariant under constant $\varepsilon$, and for local $\varepsilon(x)$ its first-order change is $\int \partial_\mu\varepsilon\, j^\mu\, d^dx$, which defines the current $j^\mu$ of the [continuous symmetry](c:continuous-symmetry).
The measure $\mathcal{D}\phi$ of the [path integral](c:path-integral) is invariant under $\phi \mapsto \phi + \varepsilon\,\delta\phi$.
The fields and $\varepsilon$ decay at infinity, so integration by parts has no boundary term.

conclusion: The [correlation functions](c:correlation-function) of the fields obey the stated Ward identity.

proofs.name: Local change of variables
proofs.slogan: Substitute a local symmetry transformation in the path integral, expand to first order, and use that the function $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary.
proofs.scope: A formal derivation without renormalization; an anomaly is exactly a failure of the invariance of the measure. For an arbitrary shift of the field, the same argument gives the Schwinger-Dyson equation.

roles.why: It gives the first-order change of the action as an integral of $\partial_\mu\varepsilon\, j^\mu$.
It removes the Jacobian, so the substituted integral equals the original one.
It lets integration by parts move the derivative from $\varepsilon$ to the current.

steps.slogan: Write the [correlation function](c:correlation-function) as a [path integral](c:path-integral) with weight $e^{iS/\hbar}$.
steps.detail: Put $F[\phi] = \phi(x_1)\cdots\phi(x_n)$. Then $\langle F\rangle = Z^{-1}\int \mathcal{D}\phi\, F[\phi]\, e^{iS[\phi]/\hbar}$, and a change of the integration variable does not change this value.

steps.slogan: Substitute the local transformation $\phi \mapsto \phi + \varepsilon\,\delta\phi$ in the integral.
steps.detail: The measure is invariant, so $\int \mathcal{D}\phi\, F[\phi]\, e^{iS[\phi]/\hbar} = \int \mathcal{D}\phi\, F[\phi + \varepsilon\delta\phi]\, e^{iS[\phi + \varepsilon\delta\phi]/\hbar}$ for every function $\varepsilon(x)$.

steps.slogan: Expand both factors to first order in $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: The change of $F$ is $\sum_k \varepsilon(x_k)\,\phi(x_1)\cdots\delta\phi(x_k)\cdots\phi(x_n)$. The change of the exponent is $\tfrac{i}{\hbar}\int \partial_\mu\varepsilon\, j^\mu\, d^dx$, multiplied by $F$. The terms of order $\varepsilon$ add up to zero.

steps.slogan: Integrate by parts to move the derivative from $\varepsilon$ to the current.
steps.detail: Without boundary terms, $\int \partial_\mu\varepsilon\, j^\mu = -\int \varepsilon\,\partial_\mu j^\mu$. The first-order condition becomes $\int \varepsilon(x)\,B(x)\, d^dx = 0$ with $B(x) = \sum_k \delta(x - x_k)\langle \cdots\delta\phi(x_k)\cdots\rangle - \tfrac{i}{\hbar}\langle \partial_\mu j^\mu(x)\,F\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Use the arbitrary function $\varepsilon$ to remove the integral over $x$.
steps.detail: The integral vanishes for every $\varepsilon$, so $B(x) = 0$ at every $x$. Multiplying by $i\hbar$ gives $\langle \partial_\mu j^\mu(x)\,F\rangle = -i\hbar\sum_k \delta(x - x_k)\langle \cdots\delta\phi(x_k)\cdots\rangle$, which is the Ward identity.

concepts.c:continuous-symmetry: The symmetry supplies the current and the first-order change of the action.
concepts.c:path-integral: The correlation functions and the change of variables live in the path integral.
concepts.c:correlation-function: The identity relates correlation functions with a current inserted.

source.note: The formal path-integral derivation of the Ward-Takahashi identity, as in Peskin and Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory, chapter 9.

statement: For every integer $k \ge 1$ there is an integer $s = s(k)$ such that every [natural number](c:natural-number) is a sum of at most $s$ $k$-th powers of natural numbers.

hypotheses.text: The exponent $k$ is a positive integer.

conclusion: Every natural number is a sum of at most $s(k)$ $k$-th powers.

proofs.name: Hardy-Littlewood circle method
proofs.slogan: Count the representations by an integral over the circle, show that the major arcs give a positive main term, and show that the minor arcs are smaller.
proofs.scope: An outline of the circle method proof; the steps on the arcs and on the singular series rest on the cited work. The case $k = 2$ is Lagrange's four-square theorem, and Hilbert gave the first proof in 1909 by another route.

roles.why: The exponent $k$ fixes the sum $f$ and the size of Weyl's saving on the minor arcs.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to numbers larger than a fixed bound $N_0$.
steps.detail: A number $N \le N_0$ is a sum of $N$ copies of $1^k$. So it is enough to find $s$ and $N_0$ such that every $N > N_0$ is a sum of $s$ $k$-th powers, where $0^k$ is allowed.

steps.slogan: Write the number of representations as an integral over the unit circle.
steps.detail: Put $P = \lfloor N^{1/k} \rfloor$, $e(x) = e^{2\pi i x}$ and $f(\alpha) = \sum_{0 \le n \le P} e(\alpha n^k)$, an [exponential sum](c:exponential-sum). Orthogonality of $e(\alpha m)$ gives $r_s(N) = \int_0^1 f(\alpha)^s e(-N\alpha)\, d\alpha$, the number of solutions of $n_1^k + \dots + n_s^k = N$.

steps.slogan: Approximate the sum $f$ near rationals with small denominator.
steps.detail: Near $a/q$ with $q$ small, $f$ is close to $q^{-1}S(q,a)\,v(\beta)$ with a complete exponential sum $S$ and an integral $v$. These major arcs contribute $\mathfrak{S}(N)\,\Gamma(1 + 1/k)^s\,\Gamma(s/k)^{-1} N^{s/k - 1}$ plus a smaller error, where $\mathfrak{S}$ is the singular series.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum $f$ on the remaining arcs by Weyl's inequality.
steps.detail: Away from rationals with small denominator, Weyl's differencing inequality gives $|f(\alpha)| \ll P^{1-\delta}$ with $\delta = \delta(k) > 0$. Combined with a mean value bound for $\int |f|^{2^k}$, the minor arcs contribute $o(N^{s/k-1})$ once $s > 2^k$.

steps.slogan: Show that the singular series stays above a positive constant.
steps.detail: The series $\mathfrak{S}(N)$ is a product of $p$-adic densities. For $s$ large in terms of $k$, each density is positive because solutions modulo $p$ lift to solutions modulo $p^j$ by Hensel's lemma, so $\mathfrak{S}(N) \ge c(s,k) > 0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the arcs to get a positive count for every large $N$.
steps.detail: The two kinds of arcs give $r_s(N) = \mathfrak{S}(N)\,\Gamma(1+1/k)^s\,\Gamma(s/k)^{-1}N^{s/k-1} + o(N^{s/k-1})$. The main term is at least $cN^{s/k-1}$, so $r_s(N) > 0$ for $N > N_0$. With step 1, every natural number is a sum of at most $\max(s, N_0)$ $k$-th powers.

concepts.c:natural-number: The claim is a bound on the number of powers needed for each natural number.
concepts.c:exponential-sum: The sum $f$ turns the counting problem into an integral of exponential sums.

source.ref: R. C. Vaughan, The Hardy-Littlewood Method, 2nd edition, Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics 125, Cambridge University Press, 1997
source.note: Chapters 2 and 4 treat Weyl's inequality and the major arcs for Waring's problem. The outline follows Hardy and Littlewood, who proved finiteness of $g(k)$ by the circle method after Hilbert's proof of 1909.

statement: Let $G$ be a [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) with parts $A$ and $B$ of sizes $m$ and $n$. Suppose that no $s$ vertices of $A$ have $t$ common neighbours in $B$, where $s, t \ge 1$. Then $G$ has at most $(t-1)^{1/s}\, m\, n^{1-1/s} + (s-1)\,n$ edges.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is [bipartite](c:bipartite-graph) with parts $A$ and $B$ of sizes $m$ and $n$.
No $s$ vertices of $A$ have $t$ common neighbours in $B$, so $G$ has no $K_{s,t}$ with its $s$ vertices in $A$, and $s, t \ge 1$.

conclusion: The number of edges of $G$ is at most $(t-1)^{1/s}\, m\, n^{1-1/s} + (s-1)\,n$.

proofs.name: Double counting of stars
proofs.slogan: Count the pairs of a vertex of $B$ and an $s$-set of its neighbours, and bound the count above and below.
proofs.scope: The upper bound of Kővári, Sós and Turán; the exact value of the Zarankiewicz number is open in general. For $m = n$ the bound is $O(n^{2-1/s})$.

roles.why: All edges join $B$ to $A$, so the degrees of the vertices of $B$ add up to the edge count.
Each $s$-set of $A$ has at most $t-1$ common neighbours, which bounds the count from above.

steps.slogan: Count the pairs of a vertex of $B$ and an $s$-set of its neighbours.
steps.detail: Let $d(u)$ be the degree of $u \in B$. The pairs $(u, S)$ with $S \subseteq N(u)$ and $|S| = s$ number $\sum_{u \in B}\binom{d(u)}{s}$. Each $s$-set $S \subseteq A$ has at most $t - 1$ common neighbours, so the sum is at most $(t-1)\binom{m}{s}$, a count with [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient).

steps.slogan: Replace the degrees by their average with Jensen's inequality.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi(x) = x(x-1)\cdots(x-s+1)/s!$ for $x \ge s-1$ and $\varphi(x) = 0$ for $x < s-1$. This function is [convex](c:convex-function) and equals $\binom{d}{s}$ at every integer $d \ge 0$. With $e = \sum_u d(u)$, Jensen gives $n\,\varphi(e/n) \le \sum_u \binom{d(u)}{s} \le (t-1)\binom{m}{s}$.

steps.slogan: Bound both sides of the inequality by powers.
steps.detail: Use $\binom{m}{s} \le m^s/s!$. If $x = e/n \ge s-1$, then $\varphi(x) \ge (x-s+1)^s/s!$. So $(x - s + 1)^s \le (t-1)\,m^s/n$.

steps.slogan: Solve the inequality for the number of edges $e$.
steps.detail: The previous bound gives $x \le s - 1 + (t-1)^{1/s}\, m\, n^{-1/s}$, so $e = nx \le (s-1)\,n + (t-1)^{1/s}\, m\, n^{1-1/s}$. If $x < s - 1$, then $e < (s-1)\,n$ and the bound holds already.

concepts.c:bipartite-graph: Every edge ends in both parts, so degrees on one side count all edges.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The counts of $s$-sets are binomial coefficients.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity lets Jensen replace the degrees by their average.

source.note: The double count of Kővári, Sós and Turán, On a problem of K. Zarankiewicz, Colloquium Mathematicum 3 (1954), 50-57.

statement: Every positive integer $n$ is a sum of distinct [Fibonacci numbers](c:fibonacci-numbers) $F_k$ with $k \ge 2$ and no two consecutive indices, and this sum is unique.

hypotheses.text: The number $n$ is a positive integer.

conclusion: There is exactly one list of indices $k_1 > k_2 > \dots > k_r \ge 2$ with $k_i - k_{i+1} \ge 2$ and $n = F_{k_1} + \dots + F_{k_r}$.

formal.difference: The declaration is an equivalence between all natural numbers (zero gives the empty list) and lists of indices that decrease by at least two and stay at least two. Existence and uniqueness are its two inverse laws.

proofs.name: Greedy representation
proofs.slogan: Take the largest Fibonacci number at most $n$, repeat on the remainder, and show that a non-consecutive sum is smaller than the next Fibonacci number.
proofs.scope: Positive $n$; zero is the empty sum. The proof follows mathlib: the greedy function and its two inverse laws.

roles.why: A positive number is at least $F_2 = 1$, so the largest index $a$ with $F_a \le n$ is at least $2$.

steps.slogan: Take the largest index $a$ with $F_a \le n$.
steps.detail: Let $a$ be the largest index with $F_a \le n$, so $F_a \le n < F_{a+1}$. The [greedy algorithm](c:greedy-algorithm) starts the representation of $n$ with $F_a$ and continues with a representation of $n - F_a$.

steps.slogan: Show that the remainder $n - F_a$ needs only indices at most $a - 2$.
steps.detail: From $n < F_{a+1} = F_a + F_{a-1}$ we get $n - F_a < F_{a-1}$. So the largest index $b$ with $F_b \le n - F_a$ has $b < a - 1$, that is $b \le a - 2$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the greedy step on the remainder by strong induction.
steps.detail: The remainder $n - F_a$ is smaller than $n$ because $F_a \ge 1$. By induction it has a representation with top index at most $a - 2$, and a remainder of zero is the empty sum. Putting $F_a$ in front gives a representation of $n$ whose indices differ by at least two.

steps.slogan: Show that a non-consecutive sum with top index $a$ is less than $F_{a+1}$.
steps.detail: Induct on the number of terms. The rest of the sum has top index at most $a - 2$, so it is less than $F_{a-1}$. Hence the whole sum is less than $F_a + F_{a-1} = F_{a+1}$.

steps.slogan: Show that every representation of $n$ has top index $a$, then strip it.
steps.detail: A representation with top index $c$ has $F_c \le n < F_{c+1}$ by the bound, so $c$ is the largest index with $F_c \le n$, which is $a$. Removing $F_a$ leaves a representation of $n - F_a$, which is unique by induction.

steps.slogan: Join existence and uniqueness into one equivalence between numbers and representations.
steps.detail: The greedy map sends $n$ to a representation, and summing a representation gives back $n$. Any representation of $n$ equals the greedy one by the uniqueness step, so the two maps are inverse to each other.

concepts.c:fibonacci-numbers: The theorem writes every positive integer as a sum of Fibonacci numbers.
concepts.c:greedy-algorithm: The representation is built by always taking the largest Fibonacci number that fits.

source.note: mathlib defines zeckendorf by the greedy rule with Nat.greatestFib. It proves the gap lemma greatestFib_sub_fib_greatestFib_le_greatestFib, isZeckendorfRep_zeckendorf, the bound IsZeckendorfRep.sum_fib_lt, and the inverse laws sum_zeckendorf_fib and zeckendorf_sum_fib.

statement: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, $\sum_{m=k}^{n}\binom{m}{k} = \binom{n+1}{k+1}$ with [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient), where the sum is empty (zero) when $n < k$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $n$ and $k$ are [natural numbers](c:natural-number).

conclusion: The sum of $\binom{m}{k}$ over $k \le m \le n$ equals $\binom{n+1}{k+1}$.

proofs.name: Induction with Pascal's rule
proofs.slogan: Induct on $n$ from $n = k$, adding one term and using Pascal's rule.
proofs.scope: All natural numbers $n$ and $k$; the case $n < k$ is separate because the sum is empty.

roles.why: The induction runs over the natural number $n$ from the base $n = k$.

steps.slogan: Check the case $n < k$, where both sides are zero.
steps.detail: If $n < k$, the sum is empty, so it is $0$. Also $n + 1 < k + 1$, so $\binom{n+1}{k+1} = 0$.

steps.slogan: Check the base case $n = k$.
steps.detail: The sum has the single term $\binom{k}{k} = 1$. The right side is $\binom{k+1}{k+1} = 1$, so both sides agree.

steps.slogan: Add the term $m = n + 1$ and apply Pascal's rule to the right side.
steps.detail: Assume the identity for some $n \ge k$. Then $\sum_{m=k}^{n+1}\binom{m}{k} = \binom{n+1}{k+1} + \binom{n+1}{k} = \binom{n+2}{k+1}$, by the induction hypothesis and Pascal's rule $\binom{N+1}{j+1} = \binom{N}{j+1} + \binom{N}{j}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude the identity for every $n \ge k$ by induction.
steps.detail: The base case and the induction step prove the identity for all $n \ge k$. The case $n < k$ is the first step, so the identity holds for all natural numbers $n$ and $k$.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: Pascal's rule relates neighbouring binomial coefficients and drives the induction step.
concepts.c:natural-number: The induction runs over the natural number $n$.

source.note: mathlib splits on n < k with choose_eq_zero_of_lt, then runs le_induction: the base case by simp and the step with sum_insert and the Pascal rule choose_succ_succ'.

proofs.name: Largest element count
proofs.slogan: Count the $(k+1)$-element subsets of $\{1, \dots, n+1\}$ by their largest element.
proofs.scope: The case $n \ge k$; for $n < k$ both sides are zero.

roles.why: The numbers $n$ and $k$ size the ground set and the subsets.

steps.slogan: Count the $(k+1)$-element subsets of $\{1, \dots, n+1\}$ directly.
steps.detail: There are $\binom{n+1}{k+1}$ such subsets by the definition of the [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient).

steps.slogan: Sort the subsets by their largest element $m + 1$.
steps.detail: A subset with $k + 1$ distinct elements has a largest element $m + 1 \ge k + 1$, so $k \le m \le n$. Each subset has exactly one largest element.

steps.slogan: Count the subsets with largest element $m + 1$.
steps.detail: The other $k$ elements form an arbitrary $k$-element subset of $\{1, \dots, m\}$. So exactly $\binom{m}{k}$ subsets have largest element $m + 1$.

steps.slogan: Add the counts over all values of $m$.
steps.detail: The classes by largest element are disjoint and cover all subsets. Hence $\binom{n+1}{k+1} = \sum_{m=k}^{n}\binom{m}{k}$.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: Binomial coefficients count the subsets on both sides of the identity.
concepts.c:natural-number: The numbers $n$ and $k$ are natural numbers that size the subsets.

source.note: The classical hockey-stick argument: count the subsets by their largest element.

statement: Let $(C, d)$ be a nonnegative [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) of vector spaces over a field with $\sum_p \dim C^p < \infty$, and $f\colon C \to C$ a chain map. Then $\sum_p (-1)^p\operatorname{tr}(f^p \mid C^p) = \sum_p (-1)^p\operatorname{tr}(H^p(f) \mid H^p(C))$, with [traces](c:trace-of-a-matrix) of linear maps.

hypotheses.text: The total dimension $\sum_p \dim C^p$ is finite.
The map $f$ is a [chain map](c:chain-map): $f d = d f$.
The [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) is nonnegative: $C^p = 0$ for $p < 0$.

conclusion: The alternating sum of the traces of $f$ on the $C^p$ equals the alternating sum of the traces of $f$ on [cohomology](c:cohomology).

proofs.name: Filtration by cycles and boundaries
proofs.slogan: Filter each $C^p$ by boundaries and cycles, split the trace along the filtration, and telescope the boundary terms.
proofs.scope: All complexes of finite total dimension; for $f = \mathrm{id}$ the formula is the equality $\sum_p (-1)^p \dim C^p = \sum_p (-1)^p \dim H^p$ of two ways to compute the [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic).

roles.why: Finite dimension makes every trace defined and every sum finite.
The relation $f d = d f$ makes $f$ preserve cycles and boundaries and commute with $d$.
It gives $B^0 = 0$, the starting point of the telescoping sum.

steps.slogan: Filter each $C^p$ by boundaries and cycles that $f$ preserves.
steps.detail: Let $B^p = \operatorname{im} d \subseteq Z^p = \ker d \subseteq C^p$. Because $f d = d f$, $f$ maps $Z^p$ into $Z^p$ and $B^p$ into $B^p$. So $f$ acts on $B^p$, on $H^p = Z^p/B^p$ and on $C^p/Z^p$.

steps.slogan: Split the trace of $f$ on $C^p$ along the filtration.
steps.detail: In a basis adapted to $B^p \subseteq Z^p \subseteq C^p$, the matrix of $f$ is block upper triangular. Its trace is the sum of the traces on the blocks: $\operatorname{tr}(f \mid C^p) = \operatorname{tr}(f \mid B^p) + \operatorname{tr}(f \mid H^p) + \operatorname{tr}(f \mid C^p/Z^p)$.

steps.slogan: Identify $C^p/Z^p$ with $B^{p+1}$ by the differential.
steps.detail: The map $d$ induces an isomorphism $C^p/Z^p \to B^{p+1}$, and $d f = f d$ makes it commute with $f$. Conjugate maps have equal trace, so $\operatorname{tr}(f \mid C^p/Z^p) = \operatorname{tr}(f \mid B^{p+1})$.

steps.slogan: Sum with alternating signs and cancel the boundary terms.
steps.detail: Put $b_p = \operatorname{tr}(f \mid B^p)$. Then $\sum_p (-1)^p \operatorname{tr}(f \mid C^p) = \sum_p (-1)^p \operatorname{tr}(f \mid H^p) + \sum_p (-1)^p (b_p + b_{p+1})$. The last sum telescopes to $b_0 = 0$, because $C^p = 0$ for $p < 0$ and all sums are finite.

concepts.c:cochain-complex: The complex supplies the spaces $C^p$ and the differential that gives cycles and boundaries.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: The theorem compares traces, and the trace is additive on block triangular matrices.
concepts.c:chain-map: A chain map preserves cycles and boundaries, so it acts on cohomology.
concepts.c:cohomology: Cohomology is the quotient of cycles by boundaries on which $f$ acts.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: The identity map gives the equality of the two Euler characteristic sums.

source.note: The Hopf trace argument: filter by boundaries and cycles, add the traces and telescope.

statement: In the Euclidean plane, the three altitudes of a [triangle](c:triangle) pass through one point, the orthocentre. The altitude from a vertex is the line through it [perpendicular](c:perpendicular) to the opposite side.

hypotheses.text: The vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ of the [triangle](c:triangle) are not collinear.

conclusion: The altitudes from $A$, $B$ and $C$ have a common point $H$, the orthocentre.

proofs.name: Dot products
proofs.slogan: Write each altitude as a dot-product equation, and note that the three left sides add up to zero for every point.
proofs.scope: All triangles, including right and obtuse ones; for a right angle at $C$ the point $H$ is $C$. The right-triangle altitude theorem $h^2 = pq$ belongs to the same family and is not proved here.

roles.why: Non-collinear vertices make two altitudes non-parallel, so they meet.

steps.slogan: Write each altitude as a line given by a dot product.
steps.detail: Use vectors in the plane. The altitude from $A$ is the set of points $P$ with $(P - A)\cdot(B - C) = 0$, because it is [perpendicular](c:perpendicular) to the side along $B - C$. The other two altitudes are given by $(P - B)\cdot(C - A) = 0$ and $(P - C)\cdot(A - B) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the altitudes from $A$ and $B$ meet at a point $H$.
steps.detail: These two lines have normal vectors $B - C$ and $C - A$. The vectors are not parallel because $A$, $B$, $C$ are not collinear. So the lines are not parallel, and they meet at a point $H$.

steps.slogan: Check that the three dot products add up to zero for every point $P$.
steps.detail: In $(P - A)\cdot(B - C) + (P - B)\cdot(C - A) + (P - C)\cdot(A - B)$, the terms with $P$ give $P \cdot 0$. The other terms $-A\cdot B + A\cdot C - B\cdot C + B\cdot A - C\cdot A + C\cdot B$ cancel in pairs.

steps.slogan: Substitute $H$ to see that it lies on the third altitude.
steps.detail: At $P = H$ the first two dot products are zero. The identity then forces $(H - C)\cdot(A - B) = 0$, so $H$ lies on the altitude from $C$.

concepts.c:triangle: The theorem concerns the three altitudes of one triangle.
concepts.c:perpendicular: An altitude is perpendicular to a side, which becomes a zero dot product.

source.note: The classical vector proof that the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

proofs.name: Anticomplementary triangle
proofs.slogan: Build the larger triangle whose side midpoints are the vertices, so that the altitudes become its perpendicular bisectors, which meet at its circumcentre.
proofs.scope: All nondegenerate triangles; the construction needs only that the sides are pairwise non-parallel.

roles.why: Pairwise non-parallel sides make the three parallels form a triangle.

steps.slogan: Draw through each vertex the parallel to the opposite side.
steps.detail: The three parallels are pairwise non-parallel, because the sides of $ABC$ are. They form a triangle $A'B'C'$, with $B'$ and $C'$ on the parallel through $A$ to $BC$, and similarly for the other vertices.

steps.slogan: Show that $A$, $B$, $C$ are the midpoints of the sides of $A'B'C'$.
steps.detail: The lines through $B$ parallel to $CA$ and through $C$ parallel to $AB$ meet at $A' = B + C - A$, the fourth corner of a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram). In the same way $B' = C + A - B$ and $C' = A + B - C$. Then the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of $B'C'$ is $A$, and likewise for $B$ and $C$.

steps.slogan: Show that each altitude of $ABC$ is a perpendicular bisector of $A'B'C'$.
steps.detail: The side $B'C'$ passes through $A$ and is parallel to $BC$. The altitude from $A$ is [perpendicular](c:perpendicular) to $BC$, so it is perpendicular to $B'C'$ at its midpoint $A$.

steps.slogan: Intersect the perpendicular bisectors at the circumcentre of $A'B'C'$.
steps.detail: The perpendicular bisectors of $B'C'$ and $C'A'$ are not parallel, so they meet at a point $O$ with $OB' = OC'$ and $OC' = OA'$. Then $OA' = OB'$, so $O$ also lies on the perpendicular bisector of $A'B'$. Hence $O$, the [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) of $A'B'C'$, lies on all three altitudes of $ABC$.

concepts.c:triangle: The proof builds a second triangle around the given one.
concepts.c:perpendicular: The altitudes are perpendicular to the sides of the larger triangle.
concepts.c:parallelogram: Parallelograms locate the corners of the larger triangle.
concepts.c:midpoint: The vertices of $ABC$ are the midpoints of the sides of $A'B'C'$.
concepts.c:circumcenter: The circumcentre of the larger triangle is the common point of the altitudes.

source.note: The classical proof by the anticomplementary triangle, with the orthocentre as the circumcentre of the larger triangle.

statement: Take $\dot x = f(x) + \sum_{i=1}^m g_i(x)u_i$ with smooth $f$, $g_i$ and $f(0) = 0$. A $C^1$ [control-Lyapunov function](c:lyapunov-function) with the small control property exists if and only if some [feedback](c:feedback-control) $u(x)$, continuous at $0$ and [locally Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}$, makes the origin globally asymptotically stable.

hypotheses.text: The system is control affine, with smooth $f$ and $g_i$ and $f(0) = 0$.

conclusion: A control-Lyapunov function with the small control property exists if and only if a stabilizing feedback of this kind exists.

proofs.name: Convex selection and converse Lyapunov theorem
proofs.slogan: Admissible controls form a convex set for each state, a partition of unity glues them into a feedback, and a converse Lyapunov theorem gives the other direction.
proofs.scope: An outline of both directions; the first is a convexity and partition-of-unity argument, and the second rests on a converse Lyapunov theorem from the cited work. A control-Lyapunov function $V$ is positive definite and proper, and for each $x \ne 0$ some $u$ gives $\dot V = L_fV + \sum_i u_i L_{g_i}V < 0$.

roles.why: The affine form makes the decrease condition linear in $u$, so the admissible controls are convex.

steps.slogan: State the decrease condition as a linear inequality in $u$.
steps.detail: Put $a(x) = L_fV(x)$ and $b_i(x) = L_{g_i}V(x)$; both are continuous because $V$ is $C^1$. A control $u$ makes $V$ decrease at $x \ne 0$ exactly when $a(x) + b(x)\cdot u < 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the admissible controls form a nonempty convex set that varies openly.
steps.detail: For $x \ne 0$, the set $K(x) = \{u : a(x) + b(x)\cdot u < 0\}$ is an open half-space, or all of $\mathbb{R}^m$ when $b(x) = 0$, so it is a [convex set](c:convex-set). It is nonempty because $V$ is a control-Lyapunov function. If $u_0 \in K(x_0)$, then $u_0 \in K(x)$ for all $x$ near $x_0$, by continuity of $a$ and $b$.

steps.slogan: Glue local constant controls into one feedback with a partition of unity.
steps.detail: Cover $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}$ by open sets $N_j$ with constants $u_j \in K(x)$ for all $x \in N_j$. A smooth [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) $\{\varphi_j\}$ gives $u(x) = \sum_j \varphi_j(x)u_j \in K(x)$, smooth off the origin. The small control property lets Artstein choose the $u_j$ small near $0$, so $u$ is continuous at $0$ with $u(0) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the closed loop decreases $V$ and drives every solution to the origin.
steps.detail: Along the closed loop $\dot V = a + b\cdot u(x) < 0$ for $x \ne 0$. On each compact shell $\{r \le V \le R\}$ the derivative is at most some $-c < 0$, so $V$ falls below every positive level. Properness bounds the solutions and positive definiteness gives stability, so the origin is globally asymptotically stable.

steps.slogan: Go back from a stabilizing feedback to a control-Lyapunov function.
steps.detail: A converse Lyapunov theorem (Massera, Kurzweil) applied to the closed loop gives a $C^1$ positive definite proper $V$ with $\dot V < 0$ off the origin. This $V$ satisfies $a + b\cdot u(x) < 0$, so it is a control-Lyapunov function. Continuity of $u$ at $0$ with $u(0) = 0$ gives the small control property.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 build a stabilizing feedback from a control-Lyapunov function, and step 5 builds a control-Lyapunov function from a stabilizing feedback. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:lyapunov-function: A control-Lyapunov function is the object that exists on one side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:feedback-control: The stabilizing feedback is the object that exists on the other side.
concepts.c:lipschitz-continuous-function: Local Lipschitz continuity makes the closed-loop solutions unique away from the origin.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of the admissible controls allows averaging local choices into one.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: The partition of unity glues local constant controls into a smooth feedback.

source.ref: Z. Artstein, Stabilization with relaxed controls, Nonlinear Analysis: Theory, Methods and Applications 7 (1983), 1163-1173
source.note: Artstein proves both directions. E. D. Sontag, Systems and Control Letters 13 (1989), 117-123, gives an explicit formula for the feedback.

statement: Let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open [unit disc](c:unit-disc) with $f'(0) = 1$. Then $f$ is injective on some open set $U$ of the disc, and $f(U)$ contains a disc of radius $1/16$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open [unit disc](c:unit-disc).
The derivative satisfies $f'(0) = 1$.

conclusion: Some open set $U$ of the unit disc has $f$ [univalent](c:univalent-function) on $U$ and $f(U)$ containing a disc of radius $1/16$.

proofs.name: Maximal weighted derivative and the Schwarz lemma
proofs.slogan: Move to the point of largest weighted derivative, normalize there, and use the Schwarz lemma to get an injective map with a large image.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the constant $1/16$ that this proof gives; the same argument with $h(z) = f(rz)/r$ gives every constant below $1/8$. The best constant is larger still, and its exact value is open.

roles.why: Holomorphy makes the rescaled function holomorphic on the closed disc and allows the Schwarz lemma.
The normalization $f'(0) = 1$ makes the maximum of the weighted derivative at least $1$.

steps.slogan: Rescale $f$ to a function $h$ that is holomorphic on the closed unit disc.
steps.detail: Put $h(z) = 2f(z/2)$. It is holomorphic on $|z| < 2$, hence on the closed disc, and $h'(0) = 1$. If $h$ is injective on a set $V$ and $h(V)$ contains a disc of radius $1/8$, then $f$ is injective on $V/2$ and $f(V/2) = h(V)/2$ contains a disc of radius $1/16$.

steps.slogan: Find the point where $(1 - |z|)\,|h'(z)|$ is largest and bound $h'$ near it.
steps.detail: The function $\mu(z) = (1 - |z|)|h'(z)|$ is continuous on the closed disc, vanishes on the circle, and has $\mu(0) = 1$. Take a maximum point $a$ with $|a| < 1$, and put $\rho = 1 - |a|$ and $M = \rho|h'(a)| \ge 1$. For $|z - a| < \rho/2$ we have $1 - |z| > \rho/2$, so $|h'(z)| < 2M/\rho = 2|h'(a)|$.

steps.slogan: Normalize at $a$ and bound $|\varphi' - 1|$ with the Schwarz lemma.
steps.detail: Let $c = \rho h'(a)/2$ and $\varphi(w) = (h(a + \rho w/2) - h(a))/c$, so $\varphi(0) = 0$, $\varphi'(0) = 1$ and $|\varphi'| < 2$ on $|w| < 1$. The map $u = (\varphi'/2 - 1/2)/(1 - \varphi'/4)$ sends the disc into itself and fixes $0$, so $|u(w)| \le |w|$ by the Schwarz lemma. Solving for $\varphi'$ gives $|\varphi'(w) - 1| \le \tfrac32|w|/(1 - |w|/2) < 1$ for $|w| < 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi$ is injective on $|w| < 1/2$ with an image containing the disc of radius $1/4$.
steps.detail: On $|w| < 1/2$ we have $\operatorname{Re}\varphi' > 0$, so $\varphi(w_1) - \varphi(w_2) = (w_1 - w_2)\int_0^1 \varphi'(w_2 + t(w_1 - w_2))\,dt \ne 0$ for $w_1 \ne w_2$. For $|w| = r < 1/2$, integrating $\varphi' - 1$ gives $|\varphi(w)| \ge r - \tfrac34 r^2/(1 - r/2)$, which tends to $1/4$. The open image of $|w| < r$ contains $0$ and its boundary misses the disc of this radius, so it contains that disc.

steps.slogan: Transport the result back to $h$ and to $f$ by affine changes of variable.
steps.detail: The map $w \mapsto h(a + \rho w/2) = h(a) + c\varphi(w)$ is injective on $|w| < 1/2$, with $|c| = M/2 \ge 1/2$. Its image contains a disc of radius $|c|/4 \ge 1/8$. So $h$ is injective on $V = \{|z - a| < \rho/4\}$ inside the unit disc, and the rescaling of step 1 gives $U = V/2$ for $f$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives the derivative bounds and the Schwarz lemma.
concepts.c:unit-disc: The weighted derivative is largest inside the disc and vanishes on its boundary.
concepts.c:univalent-function: The normalized map is shown injective on a smaller disc.

source.note: The classical proof by the maximum of (1-|z|)|f'(z)| and the Schwarz lemma, in the style of Landau; the constants are computed here.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite [connected graph](c:connected-graph) with [maximum degree](c:maximum-degree) $\Delta$ that is neither a [complete graph](c:complete-graph) nor an odd cycle. Then the [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) of $G$ is at most $\Delta$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite and [connected](c:connected-graph).
Every vertex of $G$ has at most $\Delta$ neighbours, and some vertex has exactly $\Delta$.
The graph $G$ is not a [complete graph](c:complete-graph).
The graph $G$ is not a cycle of odd length.

conclusion: The vertices of $G$ have a proper coloring with $\Delta$ colors.

proofs.name: Lovász's greedy argument
proofs.slogan: Colour greedily in order of decreasing distance from a root, and place a repeated colour on two neighbours of the last vertex when the graph is regular.
proofs.scope: Finite simple graphs. The case $\Delta \le 2$ is direct; for $\Delta \ge 3$ the proof splits into non-regular graphs, regular graphs with a cut vertex and 2-connected regular graphs.

roles.why: Connectedness gives distances to the root, so every vertex but the root has a neighbour closer to it.
At most $\Delta$ neighbours leave a free color among $\Delta$ whenever one neighbour is uncolored or two share a color.
A connected graph that is not complete has a path $a\,v\,b$ with $a, b$ non-adjacent.
The odd cycle is the one graph of maximum degree $2$ that needs three colors.

steps.slogan: Colour the connected graphs of maximum degree at most $2$ directly.
steps.detail: A connected graph with $\Delta \le 2$ is a single vertex, a path or a cycle. A single vertex and $K_2$ are complete, a path or an even cycle has a proper 2-coloring, and an odd cycle is excluded. So we may assume $\Delta \ge 3$.

steps.slogan: Colour greedily from the far end of a distance ordering toward a root.
steps.detail: Let $H$ be connected with maximum degree at most $\Delta$, and let $v$ have degree below $\Delta$ in $H$. Order the vertices by decreasing distance from $v$ and apply the [greedy algorithm](c:greedy-algorithm) with $\Delta$ colors. A vertex $u \ne v$ has a later neighbour closer to $v$, so it sees at most $\Delta - 1$ colors, and $v$ sees fewer than $\Delta$.

steps.slogan: Split a regular graph at a cut vertex and colour the pieces.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be $\Delta$-regular with a cut vertex $v$ and components $C_1, \dots, C_r$ of $G - v$, with $r \ge 2$. In $G_i = G[C_i \cup \{v\}]$ the vertex $v$ has degree below $\Delta$, so step 2 colors $G_i$ with $\Delta$ colors. Permute the colors so that $v$ has the same color in every $G_i$, and join the colorings.

steps.slogan: Find a vertex $v$ with non-adjacent neighbours $a, b$ such that $G - \{a, b\}$ is connected.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be 2-connected, $\Delta$-regular and not complete. If $G$ is 3-connected, take a path $a\,v\,b$ with $a, b$ non-adjacent. Otherwise take $v$ so that $G - v$ has a cut vertex, and $a, b$ neighbours of $v$ inside two different end blocks of $G - v$; then $G - \{a, b\}$ stays connected through a third neighbour of $v$.

steps.slogan: Colour $a$ and $b$ alike, then the rest by decreasing distance from $v$.
steps.detail: Give $a$ and $b$ the color 1; they are not adjacent. Order $G - \{a, b\}$ by decreasing distance from $v$ and colour greedily. Each vertex $u \ne v$ has a later neighbour, so it sees at most $\Delta - 1$ colors, and $v$ has two neighbours of color 1, so it also sees at most $\Delta - 1$ colors.

steps.slogan: Combine the cases into a $\Delta$-coloring of $G$.
steps.detail: If $G$ is not regular, pick $v$ of degree below $\Delta$ and apply step 2. If $G$ is regular with a cut vertex, use step 3; otherwise use steps 4 and 5. With step 1, every graph in the theorem has a proper coloring with $\Delta$ colors.

concepts.c:connected-graph: Distances to a root exist only in a connected graph.
concepts.c:maximum-degree: The bound $\Delta$ on degrees leaves a free color for each vertex.
concepts.c:complete-graph: Complete graphs need $\Delta + 1$ colors, so the proof must exclude them.
concepts.c:chromatic-number: The theorem bounds the least number of colors by $\Delta$.
concepts.c:greedy-algorithm: Greedy coloring in a good order uses at most $\Delta$ colors.

source.note: L. Lovász, Three short proofs in graph theory, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 19 (1975), 269-271.

statement: Let $R \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a closed [rectangle](c:rectangle) with sides parallel to the axes. If $f$ is continuous on $R$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the interior of $R$, then the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) $\oint_{\partial R} f(z)\,dz$ is $0$.

hypotheses.text: The set $R = [a,b] \times [c,d]$ is a closed [rectangle](c:rectangle) in the complex plane.
The function $f$ is continuous on $R$.
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the interior of $R$.

conclusion: The integral of $f$ over the boundary of $R$, taken once counterclockwise, is zero.

formal.difference: The declaration writes the boundary integral as four interval integrals between opposite corners $z$ and $w$ in either order, and lets $f$ take values in a complex Banach space. The case with countably many exceptional points is a separate declaration.

proofs.name: Divergence theorem on the rectangle
proofs.slogan: Write the boundary integral as the integral of a divergence over the rectangle, and show that this divergence is zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for either orientation of the corners. The proof follows mathlib, which gets the divergence theorem from box integrals and needs no continuity of the derivative.

roles.why: The divergence theorem is applied on the rectangle $R$, whose boundary has four sides.
Continuity on the closed rectangle gives the boundary values in the divergence theorem.
Complex differentiability inside makes the derivative complex linear, so the divergence vanishes.

steps.slogan: Show that $f_y = i f_x$ at every interior point.
steps.detail: At each interior point $f$ is real differentiable, and its derivative is multiplication by the complex number $f'(z)$. So the partial derivatives satisfy $\partial_y f = i\,\partial_x f$.

steps.slogan: Build the plane field $(P, Q) = (-if, f)$ and show that its divergence is zero.
steps.detail: On the interior, $P_x + Q_y = -i f_x + f_y = -i f_x + i f_x = 0$. Both $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $R$ and differentiable inside, as the divergence theorem requires.

steps.slogan: Apply the divergence theorem on the rectangle to the field $(P, Q)$.
steps.detail: The theorem equates the integral of $P_x + Q_y$ over $R$ with four side integrals of $P$ and $Q$. With $P = -if$ and $Q = f$, the four side integrals add up to minus the integral of $f$ around $\partial R$. The divergence is $0$, so it is integrable.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the boundary integral is zero.
steps.detail: The integral of the zero divergence over $R$ is $0$. So minus the integral of $f$ around $\partial R$ is $0$, and $\oint_{\partial R} f\,dz = 0$.

concepts.c:rectangle: The theorem and the divergence theorem both live on a rectangle.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The derivative of a holomorphic function is complex linear, which kills the divergence.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The boundary integral is the contour integral around the rectangle.

source.note: mathlib reduces to integral_boundary_rect_of_hasFDerivAt_real_off_countable, which applies the plane divergence theorem integral2_divergence_prod_of_hasFDerivAt_off_countable to the field (-I * f, f); the divergence vanishes by complex linearity of the derivative.

proofs.name: Goursat subdivision
proofs.slogan: Bisect the rectangle again and again, keep the part with the largest integral, and bound it by the linear approximation at the limit point.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 4 treat a rectangle inside the open set where $f$ is holomorphic; step 5 reaches the closed rectangle by continuity. A degenerate rectangle has a boundary integral that cancels.

roles.why: A rectangle splits into four congruent rectangles whose inner edges cancel.
Uniform continuity on the closed rectangle lets the inner rectangles approach the boundary.
Differentiability at the limit point gives the linear approximation with a small error.

steps.slogan: Bisect the rectangle into four and keep the part with the largest integral.
steps.detail: Let $I(R) = \oint_{\partial R} f\,dz$. Joining the four boundaries cancels the inner edges, so $I(R)$ is the sum of the four integrals over the parts. One part has $|I| \ge |I(R)|/4$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the bisection to get nested rectangles that shrink to one point.
steps.detail: This gives $R \supset R_1 \supset R_2 \supset \cdots$ with $|I(R_n)| \ge 4^{-n}|I(R)|$, diameter $d/2^n$ and perimeter $p/2^n$. The compact sets $R_n$ have a common point $z_0$.

steps.slogan: Approximate $f$ near $z_0$ by its linear part.
steps.detail: Because $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) at $z_0$, for each $\eta > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $|f(z) - f(z_0) - f'(z_0)(z - z_0)| \le \eta|z - z_0|$ for $|z - z_0| < \delta$. The linear polynomial $f(z_0) + f'(z_0)(z - z_0)$ has a primitive, so its integral around any closed rectangle is $0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integral over $R_n$ and let $\eta$ tend to zero.
steps.detail: For large $n$, $R_n$ lies in $|z - z_0| < \delta$, so $|I(R_n)| \le \eta\,(d/2^n)(p/2^n)$. Hence $|I(R)| \le 4^n|I(R_n)| \le \eta\,dp$ for every $\eta > 0$, so $I(R) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Pass from inner rectangles to the closed rectangle by continuity.
steps.detail: Move each side of $R$ inward by $\varepsilon$ to get $R_\varepsilon$ inside the interior, where steps 1 to 4 give $I(R_\varepsilon) = 0$. By uniform continuity of $f$ on $R$, $I(R_\varepsilon) \to I(R)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, so $I(R) = 0$.

concepts.c:rectangle: Rectangles can be bisected into four rectangles of the same shape.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Complex differentiability at the limit point gives the linear approximation.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The proof bounds the contour integral around nested rectangles.

source.note: Goursat's subdivision proof (Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 1 (1900), 14-16), with a limit step for a function that is only continuous on the boundary.

statement: Let $K$ be a field, $n \ge 1$ and $N = n(n+3)/2$. Any $N$ points of $K^2$ lie on a curve $p = 0$ for some nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ of degree at most $n$. If the points impose independent conditions on such polynomials, $p$ is unique up to a scalar factor.

hypotheses.text: Points $P_1, \dots, P_N$ of the plane $K^2$ are given, with $N = n(n+3)/2$.
The evaluation map $p \mapsto (p(P_1), \dots, p(P_N))$ from polynomials of degree at most $n$ to $K^N$ is onto; this is needed only for uniqueness.

conclusion: Some nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n$ vanishes at all $N$ points, and under independence it is unique up to a scalar factor.

proofs.name: Coefficient count
proofs.slogan: Count the coefficients of a curve of degree $n$, then solve a linear system that has one more unknown than equations.
proofs.scope: Existence needs no condition on the points; independence is the non-degenerate case where the curve is unique. Cramer's paradox ($n = 3$, nine points shared by two cubics) shows that independence can fail.

roles.why: The number $N = (n+1)(n+2)/2 - 1$ of points is one less than the number of coefficients.
Surjectivity of evaluation makes the rank equal $N$, which pins the kernel to one dimension.

steps.slogan: Count the monomials of degree at most $n$.
steps.detail: The space $V_n$ of [polynomials](c:polynomial) $\sum_{i+j \le n} c_{ij}x^iy^j$ has the monomials $x^iy^j$ with $i + j \le n$ as a basis. There are $\sum_{d=0}^{n}(d+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2 = N + 1$ of them, so $\dim V_n = N + 1$.

steps.slogan: Define the linear map that evaluates a polynomial at the $N$ points.
steps.detail: Let $\mathrm{ev}\colon V_n \to K^N$ send $p$ to $(p(P_1), \dots, p(P_N))$. It is a [linear map](c:linear-map), and a curve through all the points is a nonzero element of its kernel.

steps.slogan: Apply rank-nullity to the evaluation map.
steps.detail: Rank-nullity gives $\dim\ker\mathrm{ev} = (N + 1) - \operatorname{rank}\mathrm{ev}$. The rank is at most $N$, so the kernel has dimension at least $1$, and it has dimension exactly $1$ when the rank is $N$.

steps.slogan: Read off existence from the kernel and uniqueness from its dimension.
steps.detail: A nonzero vector of the kernel is a nonzero polynomial $p$ of degree at most $n$ through all $N$ points. Under independence the kernel is a line, so any two such polynomials are scalar multiples and the curve is unique.

concepts.c:polynomial: A degree $n$ curve is the zero set of a polynomial with $N+1$ coefficients.
concepts.c:linear-map: Evaluation at the points is linear in the coefficients of the polynomial.

source.note: The standard coefficient count behind Cramer's theorem on algebraic curves (Cramer, 1750).

statement: A system with Hamiltonian $H(x;\lambda)$ is driven from $\lambda_A$ to $\lambda_B$ by a protocol, starting in [canonical](c:canonical-ensemble) equilibrium at inverse temperature $\beta$. The reverse process starts in equilibrium at $\lambda_B$ with the reversed protocol. If the dynamics is microscopically reversible, then $P_F(W)/P_R(-W) = e^{\beta(W - \Delta F)}$, where $\Delta F = F_B - F_A$.

hypotheses.text: The system evolves as a [Markov process](c:markov-chain) in contact with a heat bath at inverse temperature $\beta$.

The dynamics is microscopically reversible, a path-level form of [detailed balance](c:detailed-balance): $P[\gamma \mid x_0]/P[\tilde\gamma \mid x_\tau] = e^{-\beta Q[\gamma]}$, where $Q$ is the heat absorbed by the system and $\tilde\gamma$ is the [time reversal](c:time-reversal) of the path $\gamma$.
The forward process starts in the [canonical](c:canonical-ensemble) distribution at $\lambda_A$, and the reverse process starts in the canonical distribution at $\lambda_B$.
The reverse process runs the reversed protocol $\tilde\lambda(t) = \lambda(\tau - t)$.

conclusion: The density of the work $W$ in the forward process and the density of $-W$ in the reverse process have the ratio $e^{\beta(W - \Delta F)}$.

proofs.name: Path reversal
proofs.slogan: Pair each forward path with its time reversal, compare the path and start probabilities, and let the heat cancel by the first law.
proofs.scope: The stochastic setting of Crooks, with a Hamiltonian that is even under momentum reversal. Integrating the result gives Jarzynski's equality.

roles.why: The Markov property gives well-defined path probabilities for the forward and reverse paths.
It states that the ratio of the path probabilities is $e^{-\beta Q}$.
The canonical start densities give the ratio of the start probabilities.
It makes the time reversal of a forward path a path of the reverse process.

steps.slogan: Pair each forward path with its time reversal.
steps.detail: [Time reversal](c:time-reversal) $\gamma \mapsto \tilde\gamma$ is a bijection from forward paths to reverse paths. It swaps the end points $x_0$ and $x_\tau$ and flips the sign of the energy change, of the heat and of the work. So $W[\tilde\gamma] = -W[\gamma]$.

steps.slogan: Compare the path probabilities by microscopic reversibility.
steps.detail: For a path $\gamma$ from $x_0$ to $x_\tau$, $P[\gamma \mid x_0]/P[\tilde\gamma \mid x_\tau] = e^{-\beta Q[\gamma]}$. This is the hypothesis for the [Markov](c:markov-chain) dynamics, and it is a form of [detailed balance](c:detailed-balance) for paths.

steps.slogan: Compare the equilibrium densities of the two starting points.
steps.detail: The forward start has the [canonical](c:canonical-ensemble) density $e^{-\beta H(x_0;\lambda_A)}/Z_A$ and the reverse start has $e^{-\beta H(x_\tau;\lambda_B)}/Z_B$. Their ratio is $e^{\beta[H(x_\tau;\lambda_B) - H(x_0;\lambda_A)]}\,Z_B/Z_A$, and $Z_B/Z_A = e^{-\beta\Delta F}$ because $F = -\beta^{-1}\ln Z$.

steps.slogan: Insert the first law so that the heat cancels.
steps.detail: The energy change $H(x_\tau;\lambda_B) - H(x_0;\lambda_A)$ equals $W[\gamma] + Q[\gamma]$. Multiplying the ratios of the two previous steps gives $e^{-\beta Q}\,e^{\beta(W + Q)}\,e^{-\beta\Delta F} = e^{\beta(W - \Delta F)}$ for the ratio of the probabilities of $\gamma$ and $\tilde\gamma$, starts included.

steps.slogan: Sum over all paths of work $W$ and use the bijection.
steps.detail: Reversal maps the forward paths of work $W$ onto the reverse paths of work $-W$. Every pair has the ratio $e^{\beta(W - \Delta F)}$, so summing over the pairs gives $P_F(W) = e^{\beta(W - \Delta F)}P_R(-W)$.

concepts.c:canonical-ensemble: The canonical distribution fixes the start densities and the free energy difference.
concepts.c:markov-chain: Markov dynamics gives the path probabilities that the proof compares.
concepts.c:detailed-balance: Microscopic reversibility is detailed balance applied to whole paths.
concepts.c:time-reversal: Time reversal pairs each forward path with a reverse path and flips the work.

source.note: G. E. Crooks, Physical Review E 60 (1999), 2721: microscopic reversibility together with canonical start densities.

statement: Let $f(z) = z + a_2z^2 + a_3z^3 + \cdots$ be [univalent](c:univalent-function) on the unit disc. Then $|a_n| \le n$ for every $n \ge 2$, with equality only for the Koebe function $z/(1-z)^2$ and its rotations.

hypotheses.text: The function has the expansion $f(z) = z + \sum_{n \ge 2} a_nz^n$ on the open unit disc.
The function $f$ is holomorphic and [univalent](c:univalent-function) (injective) on the unit disc.

conclusion: The coefficients satisfy $|a_n| \le n$ for all $n \ge 2$.

proofs.name: De Branges' proof by the Milin conjecture
proofs.slogan: Reduce the bound to Milin's inequality, prove that inequality along a Löwner chain with weights built from Jacobi polynomials, and pass to the limit.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the reductions, the system of weights and the Askey-Gasper inequality rest on the cited work. The equality case is part of the cited theorem.

roles.why: The coefficients $a_n$ define the Milin coefficients of $\log(f(z)/z)$.
Univalence puts $f$ in the class where slit maps are dense and Löwner chains exist.

steps.slogan: Reduce the coefficient bound to Milin's inequality.
steps.detail: Lebedev and Milin showed that Milin's conjecture implies Robertson's conjecture, which implies $|a_n| \le n$. Milin's conjecture concerns the coefficients $\gamma_k$ in $\log(f(z)/z) = 2\sum_k \gamma_k z^k$ and says $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(n - k + 1)(k|\gamma_k|^2 - 1/k) \le 0$.

steps.slogan: Embed the function in a Löwner chain of slit maps.
steps.detail: Maps onto the disc minus a slit are dense in the class of [univalent](c:univalent-function) functions, so it is enough to prove Milin's inequality for them. Such a map is the first member of a chain $f_t(z) = e^tz + \cdots$ that satisfies the [Löwner equation](c:lowner-equation).

steps.slogan: Introduce weights $\tau_{n,k}(t)$ that solve a triangular system of differential equations.
steps.detail: Let $\gamma_k(t)$ be the Milin coefficients of $f_t$. De Branges writes the Milin sum as minus the integral over $[0, \infty)$ of the derivative of $\sum_k \tau_{n,k}(t)(k|\gamma_k(t)|^2 - 1/k)$. The weights have $\tau_{n,k}(0) = n - k + 1$, tend to $0$ as $t \to \infty$, and solve a triangular system of differential equations built from Löwner's equation.

steps.slogan: Reduce the sign of the derivative to the Askey-Gasper inequality.
steps.detail: The differential equations turn the sign of the derivative into a positivity statement for a sum of Jacobi polynomials on $[-1, 1]$. This is the Askey-Gasper inequality of 1976, which the cited proof applies.

steps.slogan: Integrate over $t$ and pass to all univalent functions.
steps.detail: With a nonnegative derivative and the boundary values $\tau_{n,k}(0) = n - k + 1$ and $\tau_{n,k}(\infty) = 0$, the Milin sum is at most $0$ for the chain functions. Density of slit maps and limits in the normal family give Milin's inequality for every univalent $f$, so $|a_n| \le n$ by step 1.

concepts.c:univalent-function: Univalence is the hypothesis that puts the function in the class of the proof.
concepts.c:lowner-equation: Löwner's equation gives the differential equations behind the weights.

source.ref: L. de Branges, A proof of the Bieberbach conjecture, Acta Mathematica 154 (1985), 137-152
source.note: The steps follow de Branges' proof. C. H. FitzGerald and Ch. Pommerenke, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 290 (1985), 683-690, give a shorter account.
